messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kwame's Story

Kwame was thirty-four when he first came to the clinic, referred by his physician after a panic attack at work left him unable to complete his shift. He had been a parole officer for eight years—a job that demanded presence, authority, and composure—but the man who sat in the intake chair was visibly depleted, his shoulders hunched as though bearing an invisible weight. Two years earlier, his partner of five years had subjected him to a sustained assault that left him with three broken ribs and a fractured wrist. The attack had come without warning during what Kwame had thought was a quiet evening at home. His partner had accused him of infidelity, and when Kwame had tried to leave the room, the man had grabbed him by the throat, thrown him against the kitchen counter, and struck him repeatedly. The hospital smell—that sharp, chemical antiseptic—had been the first thing Kwame registered when paramedics arrived. He had pressed his face into the stretcher to escape it, but the odor had lodged itself somewhere deep in his nervous system, becoming a permanent marker of that night's terror.

Since then, Kwame's world had contracted in ways he could barely articulate. The hospital smell alone—encountered in the clinic waiting room, in a colleague's hand sanitizer, even in the bathroom of the parole office—triggered an immediate cascade of threat detection. His body would stiffen, his breathing would shallow, and suddenly he was scanning the room for exits and assessing which men nearby might pose a danger. The smell carried with it not just memory but a full sensory reincarnation: he could taste the blood in his mouth as it had tasted that night, metallic and terrifying. The memory did not feel like something past. It felt like it was happening again, right then, in real time. Being looked at in a way he perceived as sexual—a client's lingering gaze, a stranger's appraisal—triggered the same response. He had come to believe that being desired meant being vulnerable, that attraction was a precursor to violence. And the most paralyzing trigger of all was being alone with other men. At work, Kwame had begun to dread the one-on-one parole check-ins that formed the core of his job. Each meeting with a male parolee sent his nervous system into overdrive, even though his rational mind knew these men posed no threat. His body remained on constant alert, muscles coiled, ready to react to danger that his hypervigilant scanning insisted might materialize at any moment.

The memory's vividness—the way it felt present and happening rather than safely in the past—had gradually convinced Kwame that his life was fundamentally destroyed. How could he continue in a job that required him to sit alone with men when his own body betrayed him with panic? How could he maintain his relationship when he had begun to recoil from his new partner's touch, certain that intimacy would inevitably lead to harm? What had happened to him was profoundly unfair, and nothing had been done about it; his ex-partner had never faced consequences, had moved on, while Kwame remained trapped in the moment of violence. These thoughts—that his life was no longer worth living, that he had been irreparably damaged—had taken root and grown stronger with each passing week. They fed into a pattern of avoidance that had become increasingly rigid. He pushed away any moment of happiness or connection, convinced that positive feelings were dangerous, that lowering his guard would invite catastrophe. He avoided eye contact with colleagues and clients, terrified that being truly seen might expose his weakness or invite unwanted attention. Most critically, he had begun to avoid any situation that might involve conflict or disagreement. At work, when a parolee became defensive or argumentative, Kwame would capitulate rather than assert his authority, his fear of confrontation so overwhelming that he would make exceptions to protocol simply to prevent tension from escalating.

These avoidance patterns had become self-reinforcing. By retreating from conflict, Kwame felt temporarily safer, but the relief was short-lived. His avoidance meant he never stayed in triggering situations long enough for his nervous system to learn they were safe. Instead, each encounter with a male colleague, each whiff of antiseptic, each moment of being looked at, seemed to confirm his worst beliefs: the world was dangerous, men were threats, and his life had been fundamentally altered beyond repair. His body remained locked in vigilance, scanning, watching, waiting. The intrusive memories—the taste, the sounds, the feeling of being present in that violence—would surge without warning, and his only response was to withdraw further, to avoid more, to push away the few people trying to reach him. By the time Kwame sought help, he had taken a leave of absence from work. His relationship was strained nearly to breaking. He spent most evenings in his apartment, the curtains drawn, uncertain whether he was hiding from the world or simply waiting for the next moment when his past would catch up with him. What frightened him most was the thought that this—this contracted, vigilant, isolated existence—might be all that remained of his life.
